prompt: What does a language model receive in place of a sentence?
hint: Think about what the tokenizer hands over.

choices.text: The Unicode code of each character, in order
choices.why: That is how the text is stored, not what the model reads: the tokenizer cuts pieces bigger than a character.

choices.text: A list of integers, one per piece of text
choices.why: Right. The tokenizer cuts the text into tokens and replaces each by its id.

choices.text: The words as strings, which the first layer compares
choices.why: A network computes with numbers; strings never reach it.

choices.text: One vector for the whole sentence, made by the tokenizer
choices.why: The tokenizer produces one id per piece; vectors come from the embedding table, one per token.

prompt: How many different characters did `split.py` find in the corpus?
hint: The first line it printed.

prompt: A team built a word vocabulary from its customers' e-mails in 2024. In 2026 the e-mails mention a product launched in 2025. What does the model receive for its name?
hint: What did `split.py` do with `weaver`?

choices.text: Its letters, one token each
choices.why: That is a character vocabulary, or the bottom of a subword one; a word vocabulary has no letters to fall back on.

choices.text: A new entry, added the first time the name is seen
choices.why: The vocabulary is fixed when it is built, and the model's table has no row for an entry added later.

choices.text: `<unk>`, the same as any other unseen word
choices.why: Right. Whatever the name said is lost before the first layer.

choices.text: An error, and the e-mail is skipped
choices.why: Unknown words are replaced, not refused: `split.py` printed `<unk>` and carried on.

prompt: `a` + `k` and `k` + `e` were both seen 20 times. Why was `a` + `k` merged first?
hint: Look at what `most_common` does with equal counts.

choices.text: Pairs that start a word are merged before the others
choices.why: Neither pair starts a word; position plays no part in the count.

choices.text: It was counted first, and a tie goes to the first
choices.why: Right. A different tie rule would give a different, equally valid, merge list.

choices.text: `a` + `k` was seen more often once `bakers` is counted twice
choices.why: Each word counts as often as it was seen, once per pair; both totals are 20.

choices.text: Vowels are merged into the pair before consonants
choices.why: BPE knows nothing about letters; it counts pairs.

prompt: Put in order what a trained BPE tokenizer does to a word it has never seen.
hint: Encoding replays training.
items: Split the word into its letters (or bytes)
Apply the first merge learnt, wherever its pair occurs
Apply each later merge, in the order it was learnt
Replace each resulting piece by its id

prompt: With the six merges `bpe.py` learnt, how is the new word `remake` encoded?
hint: Replay the merges in order on r, e, m, a, k, e.

choices.text: `re` and `make`, two pieces
choices.why: No merge ever made `re`; `r` + `e` was never the commonest pair.

choices.text: `r`, `e` and `make`
choices.why: Right: merges 1 and 2 give `ake`, merge 5 gives `make`, and nothing joins `r` or `e`.

choices.text: `r`, `e`, `m` and `ake`
choices.why: That stops after merge 2; merge 5 then glues `m` to `ake`.

choices.text: `<unk>`, since the word is not among the five
choices.why: BPE falls back to letters, so a new word is pieces, never a hole.

prompt: Why does a byte-level tokenizer never produce an unknown token?
hint: What is in its vocabulary before the first merge?

choices.text: It is trained on text in every language
choices.why: `tok.json` was trained on forty-five lines of English and still encoded Portuguese with no unknowns.

choices.text: It adds a new entry for each word it has not seen
choices.why: The vocabulary is fixed after training; `weaver` came out in four existing pieces.

choices.text: Its starting vocabulary holds all 256 byte values
choices.why: Right. Any text is bytes, and every byte has an entry.

choices.text: It drops the characters it cannot encode
choices.why: Nothing is dropped: `ã` became two tokens, one per byte.

prompt: Asked for 1,000 entries, the trainer stopped at 700. Why?
hint: What had every word of the corpus become by then?

choices.text: Every word was already one token
choices.why: Right. Merges never cross the pre-tokenizer's cuts, so with no pair left inside a word there was nothing to merge.

choices.text: The library caps the vocabulary for a small file
choices.why: There is no such cap; the corpus simply ran out of pairs.

choices.text: Pairs seen only once are not merged
choices.why: `Sunday`, seen once, would have merged at a larger size; the stop came from the cuts.

choices.text: Training stops early so as not to overfit the corpus
choices.why: BPE has no validation set and no notion of overfitting; it counts pairs until none remain.

prompt: In the token ` Monday`, the leading ___ belongs to the token, which is how decoding rebuilds the text without guessing.
hint: Look at the first character of ` Monday`.

prompt: Why is the id 288 not given to the network as the number 288?
hint: What would 258 and 307 be, next to it?

choices.text: Numbers that large overflow a `float32`
choices.why: A `float32` holds 288 exactly; the problem is meaning, not range.

choices.text: The network wants inputs between 0 and 1
choices.why: Dividing by 500 would fix the scale and keep the false order.

choices.text: Its order and distances would mean nothing
choices.why: Right. Ids are names, numbered by the order of training.

choices.text: PyTorch refuses integer inputs to a linear layer
choices.why: A conversion would make it run, and it would still be wrong.

prompt: A vocabulary of 2,000 tokens gets embeddings of 16 numbers each. How many parameters does the table hold?
hint: One row per token.

prompt: A batch uses 140 different tokens of a 30,000-token vocabulary. How many rows of the embedding table does its backward pass change?
hint: `lookup.py`'s last line.

choices.text: All 30,000, since every row is part of the product
choices.why: In the one-hot product a zero input gives a zero gradient, so unread rows get none.

choices.text: The 140 that were looked up
choices.why: Right, as in `rows with a gradient: 7 of 500`.

choices.text: One per sentence in the batch
choices.why: Rows belong to tokens, not to sentences.

choices.text: None until the epoch ends
choices.why: The optimiser steps after each batch; an epoch boundary changes nothing.

prompt: Why does `near.py` print the neighbours before training as well as after?
hint: ` baker` and ` rains` at 0.89.

choices.text: To check the tokenizer loaded correctly
choices.why: Loading the tokenizer is checked by the ids it gives, not by cosines of random rows.

choices.text: To see how close random vectors come by chance alone, as a baseline
choices.why: Right. In eight dimensions chance gives cosines above 0.8, so a trained one means something only against that.

choices.text: Because Adam needs a first similarity to start from
choices.why: Adam reads gradients of the loss; the neighbours are only printed.

choices.text: To show the table starts with the categories already sorted
choices.why: The untrained neighbours, `rains` for `baker`, show the opposite.

prompt: What put ` Monday` next to ` Saturday` and ` Friday` after training?
hint: The model's task was to guess a token from its neighbours.

choices.text: The tokenizer gave the days neighbouring ids
choices.why: Ids are in the order of the merges and carry no meaning.

choices.text: The shared ending `day` in their spelling
choices.why: Each is one whole token, so the model never sees their letters.

choices.text: A list of weekdays the program gave the model
choices.why: The program gives no categories; the only input is the corpus.

choices.text: They fill the same slots in the corpus's sentences
choices.why: Right: `On ___ the`. Similar company, similar guesses, similar rows.

prompt: You train `near.py`'s model on another corpus, where `violet` appears twice. Its nearest neighbour comes out at 0.85. What does that tell you?
hint: Compare with `red`, and with the untrained block.

choices.text: That the two words mean nearly the same
choices.why: 0.85 is within what chance gave untrained rows in eight dimensions.

choices.text: Little: two examples, and chance reaches 0.85 anyway
choices.why: Right. `red`, seen three times, had neighbours at 0.86 that meant nothing.

choices.text: That the model needs more dimensions to separate them
choices.why: The problem is evidence, not room: two examples are too few at any size.

choices.text: That the training diverged
choices.why: A diverging run shows in the loss, not in one word's neighbour.

prompt: Why did the Portuguese sentences cost 86 tokens where the English cost 41?
hint: What was `tok.json` trained on?

choices.text: Portuguese sentences are twice as long in characters
choices.why: They are about the same length: 37 against 32, 39 against 43.

choices.text: Its merges were learnt from English alone
choices.why: Right. No merge covers Portuguese, so its words fall back to small pieces.

choices.text: Accents are replaced by unknown tokens
choices.why: A byte-level tokenizer has no unknown token; `ã` became two byte tokens.

choices.text: Portuguese has more words per sentence
choices.why: The pairs have similar word counts; the difference is pieces per word.

prompt: Why did `' pão'` take four tokens?
hint: Compare the chars and bytes columns.

choices.text: Each letter of a Portuguese word is its own token
choices.why: `p` came with its space as one token, so it is not one per letter.

choices.text: The tilde is a separate character
choices.why: `ã` is one character here; it is two bytes, not two characters.

choices.text: ` p`, then each of the two bytes of `ã` alone, then `o`
choices.why: Right. UTF-8 spends two bytes on `ã`, and no merge joins them.

choices.text: The space before it counts as two tokens
choices.why: The space is part of the first token, ` p`.

prompt: A company moves its support chatbot from English to Portuguese, keeping a model whose tokenizer was trained mostly on English. What should it expect?
hint: Context and price are both counted in tokens.

choices.text: The same bill, since a provider charges per character
choices.why: Providers charge per token, and Portuguese needs more of them here.

choices.text: Unknown tokens wherever an accent appears
choices.why: A byte-level tokenizer encodes every accent, as extra tokens.

choices.text: Fewer turns fit in the context, and each costs more
choices.why: Right. Both scale with the token count, and the same meaning costs more tokens.

choices.text: The model refuses text outside its training language
choices.why: Any text encodes; it is read in more, smaller pieces.

prompt: Match each choice to what it does.
hint: Think of `weaver` under each.

pairs.right: Nothing unknown, and the longest sequences
Short sequences, and unseen words become <unk>
Common words whole, rare words in pieces
One row of numbers per token

prompt: Which of these did this lesson's runs show? Choose all that apply.
hint: Check each against a transcript.

choices.text: At 500 entries the corpus became 1,002 tokens
choices.why: Yes: `asked  500  learnt  500  tokens  1002`.

choices.text: The trained tokenizer turned `weaver` into `<unk>`
choices.why: No: that was the word vocabulary of `split.py`. The tokenizer gave four pieces.

choices.text: A lookup equalled the one-hot product exactly
choices.why: Yes: `equal: True`.

choices.text: After training, the nearest neighbour of `red` was `green`
choices.why: No: it was `all`, at 0.86. `red` was the failure.

choices.text: The Portuguese sentences cost more than twice the English tokens
choices.why: Yes: 86 against 41, a ratio of 2.10.
